title: Put the person before the agenda
author: Rod J. Naquin
summary: Naquin builds a case against agenda-first meeting culture in schools out of three sources, and the theory is doing real work rather than decorating a management tip. He begins by tracking down the Vygotsky line about becoming ourselves through others to its actual home, a 1931 essay where a baby's failed grasp becomes a pointing gesture only because a caregiver reads it that way first. Borges supplies the second piece, the empire whose map grew to the size of the empire and became useless, which is his figure for a leadership agenda that tries to account for every minute and every voice in advance. Bakhtin supplies the third and strongest claim, that being is communicating and that a person is never finalized, which makes pre-sorting colleagues into a yes or a resistor a category error rather than a discourtesy. The payoff is a specific talk move: ask something non-instrumental before the agenda, stay one exchange longer than instinct allows, reflect the answer back in the speaker's own words, and name the bridge out loud when you transition. He also asks leaders to resist resolving genuine disagreement into one tidy conclusion, on the grounds that polyphony is where truth comes from.
points: Corrects the provenance of a widely misattributed Vygotsky quotation and shows the original context is a claim about how a mind is built, not a slogan about teamwork.
Uses the Borges map to diagnose over-specified PLC and leadership agendas as tools that have grown too large to be usable.
Argues an agenda-first culture treats colleagues as finalized data points, which is the mechanism by which people stop being people and start being processed.
Gives a scripted talk move with a named transition line, so the human exchange is marked as connected to the task rather than a warm-up to it.
Defends leaving genuine disagreement unresolved on the table, invoking polyphony against the instinct to flatten a room into one takeaway.
quotes: The more I read, the more I realized efficacy beliefs don’t come from nowhere.
The child, he writes, “is the last to realize his own gesture.” Its meaning is made by another person first.
A map that size can’t be unfolded, can’t be carried, can’t be consulted.
When the agenda comes before the person, people stop being people and start being processed
that a colleague can be reduced in advance to what the agenda needs her to be
But nobody is finished. The teacher who seems shut down on Tuesday is not a settled data point; she’s in the middle of something you don’t know about.
Bakhtin also gives us a word for why disagreement in a room isn’t a problem to smooth over as fast as possible
You’re not discarding what they said to get to the “real” agenda; you’re marking, out loud, that the human exchange and the task are connected, not competing.
